title: Applied anatomy: scalp, pterion and the middle meningeal artery (extradural haematoma)

guidelineVersions: Wilson et al., Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med (2012)

related.why: Head injury: who needs a CT and how quickly

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in the emergency department
brief.scenario: Callum Reid, 24, was struck on the right temple by a hockey stick. He was knocked out briefly, recovered, then became drowsy 40 minutes later.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the anatomy of the scalp and skull, interpret his CT findings when the examiner reads them out, and relate them to his injury.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Name the emergency, then the layers, the pterion, the artery and the CT findings. Finish with who evacuates it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Spending the station on anatomy while the patient deteriorates, or offering to drill a burr hole yourself.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is an extradural haematoma until proven otherwise: urgent CT and neurosurgical referral."

grid.label: Recognise and escalate
grid.fail: Calls it concussion and plans ward observation.
grid.pass: Names an extradural haematoma from the lucid interval; asks for urgent CT, airway support and immediate neurosurgical referral.
grid.high: Says a lucid interval is often absent, so a falling GCS alone mandates action; arranges anaesthetic support for transfer.

grid.label: Scalp layers
grid.fail: Cannot name the five layers in order.
grid.pass: Skin, dense connective tissue, galea aponeurotica, loose areolar tissue, pericranium.
grid.high: Loose areolar layer is the danger area (emissary veins to dural sinuses); vessels held open in dense tissue bleed freely.

grid.label: Pterion
grid.fail: Cannot describe where the pterion lies or name the bones meeting there.
grid.pass: H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of sphenoid, over the anterior branch of the artery.
grid.high: Surface marking about 2.6 cm behind and 1.3 cm above the frontozygomatic suture; the adjacent squamous temporal bone is thinner still.

grid.label: Middle meningeal artery
grid.fail: Calls the bleed venous or places it beneath the dura.
grid.pass: Branch of the maxillary artery; enters via foramen spinosum; runs between skull and dura. A temporal fracture tears it.
grid.high: Arterial pressure strips dura from bone; dura is fixed at sutures, so the clot is biconvex and stops at sutures.

grid.label: Interpret the CT findings
grid.fail: Calls the collection a subdural or cannot interpret the findings.
grid.pass: Interprets the biconvex hyperdense extra-axial collection under the fracture as an extradural haematoma, with mass effect and midline shift.
grid.high: Contrasts a crescentic subdural that crosses sutures; mixed density suggests active bleeding.

grid.label: Definitive management and burr holes
grid.fail: Plans a burr hole himself without neurosurgical input.
grid.pass: Urgent craniotomy by neurosurgeons. Emergency burr hole only if transfer is impossible, on neurosurgical advice, sited over the clot on CT.
grid.high: Temporal hole just above the zygoma on the side of the clot; frontal then parietal only if needed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A blow to the temple, a lucid interval, then a falling GCS: an extradural haematoma until proven otherwise. I'd protect his airway, get an urgent CT and refer to neurosurgery immediately.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Name the layers of the scalp.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Skin, dense connective tissue, the galea aponeurotica, loose areolar tissue and pericranium.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and the greater wing of sphenoid. The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies deep to it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's a branch of the maxillary artery. It enters through foramen spinosum and runs between the skull and the dura, so a fracture here tears it.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Here are his CT findings. What do they show?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: An extradural haematoma: a biconvex hyperdense collection under the right temporal fracture, with mass effect and midline shift.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent craniotomy by the neurosurgeons. A burr hole in the ED is only for when transfer is impossible, on their advice, over the clot on the CT.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An extradural haematoma. Many patients never have a lucid interval, so his falling GCS is enough. I'd call the anaesthetist for his airway and transfer, get an urgent CT and refer to neurosurgery now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Skin, dense connective tissue, galea, loose areolar tissue, pericranium. The loose areolar layer is the danger area: emissary veins carry infection to the dural sinuses. Scalp vessels are held open in the dense layer, so they bleed freely.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Where is the pterion on the surface?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: About 2.6 cm behind and 1.3 cm above the frontozygomatic suture, which I can feel. The squamous temporal bone just behind it is thinner still.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His CT findings describe a lens-shaped clot. Why is it that shape?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Arterial pressure strips the dura off the bone. The dura is fixed at the sutures, so the clot is biconvex and stops at them.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A subdural is crescentic and crosses sutures. Mixed density inside this clot would suggest it's still bleeding.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Neurosurgery are 3 hours away and he is coning. They advise a burr hole.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: On their advice I'd make a temporal hole just above the zygoma on the side of the clot, and add frontal then parietal holes only if needed. He still goes for craniotomy.

failures.move: Treating a lucid interval and falling GCS as concussion.
failures.consequence: Delay lets the haematoma expand until he cones.

failures.move: Offering an ED burr hole without neurosurgical advice.
failures.consequence: Delays definitive craniotomy and risks a hole away from the clot.

failures.move: Describing a venous bleed beneath the dura.
failures.consequence: Confuses extradural with subdural and misses why deterioration is rapid.

failures.move: Unable to say where the pterion lies.
failures.consequence: Cannot relate the injury to the artery beneath it.

recovery.line: SCALP: skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium.

recovery.when: Asked to do a burr hole
recovery.line: Only on neurosurgical advice when transfer is impossible; he still needs a craniotomy.

knowledge.fact: Scalp: skin, dense connective tissue, galea, loose areolar tissue (danger area), pericranium.
Pterion: frontal, parietal, squamous temporal, greater wing of sphenoid; anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies deep.
Pterion centre about 2.6 cm behind and 1.3 cm above the frontozygomatic suture; bone 4.4 mm thick there, about 1 mm at the thinnest squamous temporal point.
Middle meningeal artery: maxillary artery, foramen spinosum, extradural course.
Emergency burr holes only when neurosurgery is unavailable: temporal first, above the zygoma, guided by CT.

recall.think: Temple blow, lucid interval, falling GCS: extradural haematoma, coning.
recall.say: "Extradural haematoma: urgent CT and neurosurgery now."
recall.trap: A lucid interval is often absent; a talking patient can still cone.
recall.finish: Craniotomy; burr hole only on neurosurgical advice if transfer impossible.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

partner.opening: This man was hit on the right temple and is now drowsy. What do you think has happened?

reveals.finding: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), falling from 15. Right pupil larger and sluggish.

Ask: on the side of the skull, behind the frontozygomatic suture and above the zygomatic arch, four bones meet in an H-shaped junction; on the inner surface beneath it, a branching groove runs upwards and backwards. What is this junction, which bones meet there, and what runs deep to it?

Read out: axial non-contrast CT head. Over the right temporal lobe there is a lens-shaped (biconvex), uniformly hyperdense collection between the inner table of the skull and the brain. Its margins do not cross the skull suture lines. There is a fracture of the overlying right temporal bone. The right lateral ventricle is compressed and the midline is shifted to the left.

push.question: Name the layers of the scalp.
push.expect: Skin, dense connective tissue, galea, loose areolar tissue, pericranium.

push.question: Which bones meet at the pterion, and what lies beneath?
push.expect: Frontal, parietal, squamous temporal, greater wing of sphenoid; anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

push.question: Where does the middle meningeal artery come from?
Why is an extradural clot biconvex?
push.expect: Dura is stripped from bone but held at sutures.

push.question: Who treats this and how?
push.expect: Neurosurgical craniotomy; burr hole only on advice if transfer impossible.

curveballs.prompt: He was talking normally on arrival. Does that reassure you?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No. The lucid interval is the danger; repeat GCS and pupils and act on any fall.

curveballs.prompt: Where is the danger area of the scalp, and why?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Loose areolar tissue: emissary veins let infection spread to the dural sinuses.

curveballs.prompt: How would a subdural look different?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Crescentic, crosses sutures, from torn bridging veins.
